summary: Kagan's secular realism answers Craig's grounding challenge most effectively on finite significance and prudential conflict, while Craig presses a substantial explanatory-value objection.

pro.text: God's Own holy and loving nature supplies the absolute standard
pro.context: Craig presents divine nature as the objective measure of goodness before challenging naturalistic explanations of intrinsic human worth.

con.text: it matters to them it matters to their family
con.context: Kagan answers the extinction argument by locating objective importance in the actual experience and relationships of finite sufferers.

con-harm-help-objective-value.words: Kagan proposes that wrong action harms people or unjustifiably withholds help, while right action avoids harm and provides assistance under relevant circumstances.
con-harm-help-objective-value.critique: Strongest feature: The harm-and-help account supplies concrete, intelligible moral content and directly advances the secular objective-reasons burden without pretending to deliver an exhaustive ethical theory. Principal limitation: Its references to relevant circumstances and appropriate assistance leave justification thresholds, competing harms, demandingness, and distributive priorities substantially underdefined. Live burden: The account must explain why these welfare-centered considerations possess stance-independent authority and how conflicts among victims, beneficiaries, permissions, and obligations should be resolved without merely importing disputed intuitions. Locked score: The strong performance band reflects excellent relevance, coherent practical orientation, and appropriately modest presentation, while preserving meaningful deductions for compressed foundations, incomplete boundary conditions, and limited argument for the objective authority of the proposed standard.

con-categorical-objective-reasons.words: Kagan defines objective morality as universally applicable, overriding categorical reasons whose authority does not depend on anyone's opinions, desires, projects, or goals.
con-categorical-objective-reasons.critique: Strongest feature: The formulation precisely identifies the secular realist thesis as universal, desire-independent, overriding reasons, thereby preventing objectivity from collapsing into preference, convention, or contingent motivation. Principal limitation: The passage confidently characterizes categorical authority but largely assumes the deeper metaphysical and normative explanation that would establish why such reasons exist and govern every agent. Live burden: The secular case must connect moral facts to authoritative reasons without treating their categorical status as self-certifying, while also explaining how agents identify, compare, and act upon them amid genuine disagreement. Locked score: The upper strong performance band recognizes unusually clear scope, stable terminology, direct central-burden contact, and coherent exposition, while retaining deductions because definition and illustration do not yet constitute a complete defense of categorical authority.

con-rational-contract-duty.words: Kagan offers impartial agreement among perfectly rational agents behind a veil of ignorance as a secular foundation for objective rules governing mutual conduct.
con-rational-contract-duty.critique: Strongest feature: The ideal-contract proposal offers an impartial procedure linking moral requirements to what rational agents would prescribe without knowing their identities, advantages, or vulnerabilities. Principal limitation: Perfect rationality, admissible bargaining information, agreement conditions, and the transition from hypothetical choice to categorical obligation remain insufficiently specified. Live burden: The account must show that its procedural constraints are independently justified, yield determinate principles rather than multiple reasonable settlements, and bind actual agents who never participated in the imagined agreement. Locked score: The strong performance band reflects direct engagement with the secular-duty burden, coherent procedural architecture, and appropriately illustrative calibration, while preserving deductions for compressed derivation, underdeveloped authority, and uncertainty about which substantive rules ideal bargainers would necessarily select.

con-no-personal-lawgiver-required.words: Kagan argues that genuine moral requirements need no personal legislator, just as non-contradiction governs reasoning without having been enacted by a cosmic logician.
con-no-personal-lawgiver-required.critique: Strongest feature: The non-contradiction analogy sharply challenges the inference from genuine normative authority to personal legislation and confines its conclusion to the claimed necessity of a lawgiver. Principal limitation: Logical consistency and moral obligation may differ because the latter concerns accountable interpersonal claims, permissions, blame, and authoritative demands rather than conditions of intelligible reasoning alone. Live burden: The secular position must explain whether impersonal moral reasons generate directed obligations and accountability, while the theistic position must identify a principled disanalogy instead of presupposing that every obligation resembles enacted law. Locked score: The very strong performance band reflects precise relevance, stable formulation, strong responsiveness, and charitable confrontation of the lawgiver premise, with limited deductions because the analogy undermines necessity more clearly than it establishes equivalence.

pro-objective-value-divine-nature.words: Craig grounds objective goodness in God's holy and loving nature, then argues that contingent evolutionary adaptation cannot adequately explain intrinsic human moral worth.
pro-objective-value-divine-nature.critique: Strongest feature: The move offers an intelligible positive standard in divine character and directly asks what explains intrinsic human worth rather than merely cataloguing valued capacities or inherited attitudes. Principal limitation: It shifts between grounding goodness generally and grounding persons specifically, while compressing secular realism into evolutionary preference without closely confronting irreducible value, welfare, or categorical-reason alternatives. Live burden: The theistic case must explain how divine properties establish goodness without circularity and why comparable secular stopping points are inadequate, while distinguishing evolutionary explanations of belief from defeaters for moral truth. Locked score: The strong performance band reflects central relevance, a recognizable grounding proposal, and genuine contact with secular claims, while substantial deductions remain for comparative incompleteness, overstated exclusivity, and limited representational charity.

pro-duty-divine-lawgiver.words: Craig grounds objective duties in commands necessarily expressing God's moral nature and contrasts those obligations with social conditioning, convention, and contractual agreement.
pro-duty-divine-lawgiver.critique: Strongest feature: The account clearly joins divine commands to a necessarily moral nature, avoiding a purely arbitrary decree model while directly addressing the source of categorical duty. Principal limitation: The inference from objective obligation to personal command remains substantially unsupported, and ideal rational agreement is treated too readily as ordinary social convention rather than a proposed objective procedure. Live burden: The theistic case must explain why impersonal reasons cannot obligate, how divine authority produces duties beyond identifying values, and why necessary divine character avoids merely relocating the normative foundation. Locked score: The strong performance band reflects clear construction, indispensable burden contact, and an internally intelligible command framework, while deductions remain for weak comparative engagement, compressed warrant, and incomplete answers to logical-normativity and hypothetical-contract objections.

con-reflective-agency-responsibility.words: Kagan locates moral responsibility in rational agents' capacity to reflect upon reasons and regulate conduct, distinguishing them from lions and very young children.
con-reflective-agency-responsibility.critique: Strongest feature: The reflective-agency distinction is concrete, stable, and highly responsive, explaining why responsibility attaches differently to reason-responsive adults, nonreflective animals, and immature children. Principal limitation: The account explains eligibility for responsibility more fully than it explains why reflective capacity, its possessors, or the reasons recognized have objective value and authority. Live burden: The secular case must connect deliberative control with valid moral standards and degrees of accountability, including impaired agency, while avoiding a slide from capacity to recognize reasons into a foundation for those reasons. Locked score: The very strong performance band reflects excellent directness, coherent differentiation, representative support, and measured scope, with remaining deductions because the answer resolves the agency question more decisively than the underlying value-grounding challenge.

con-rational-capacity-suffices.words: Kagan argues that evolved agents able to step back, assess standards, and recognize reasons possess the machinery needed for morality without a supernatural addition.
con-rational-capacity-suffices.critique: Strongest feature: The reply identifies a plausible naturalistic threshold for moral agency in reflective distance, standard assessment, endorsement, and responsiveness to reasons. Principal limitation: It moves too quickly from possessing deliberative machinery to having objectively authoritative standards, leaving reflective endorsement insufficiently distinguished from correct normative recognition. Live burden: The secular account must show how reflection tracks stance-independent reasons rather than rationalizing preference, and why no additional value-grounding explanation is required once reason-responsive capacities appear. Locked score: The strong performance band reflects explicit contact with the supernatural-addition challenge, coherent agency mechanics, and meaningful central-burden contribution, while deductions remain because the sufficiency claim outruns its supporting argument and only partially answers the separate question of what makes capacities or their objects objectively valuable.

pro-capacities-need-value-ground.words: Craig grants distinctive human capacities but argues that identifying reflection, love, creativity, and communication does not explain why persons possessing them are objectively valuable.
pro-capacities-need-value-ground.critique: Strongest feature: The reply precisely separates locating value-bearing characteristics from explaining their objective value, exposing an important omitted inference in the naturalistic capacity account. Principal limitation: The challenge does not itself demonstrate that an irreducible secular value fact is illegitimate or that divine nature provides a more explanatory and less primitive stopping point. Live burden: The secular side must defend its foundational stopping rule, while the theistic side must articulate comparative explanatory criteria showing why grounding value in divine nature succeeds where grounding value in persons or reasons fails. Locked score: The very strong performance band reflects diagnostic precision, excellent responsiveness, strong charity, and direct contact with a central bridge, with modest deductions because identifying an explanatory gap is not yet a complete positive demonstration of theism.

pro-extinction-undermines-significance.words: Craig argues that universal extinction and absent ultimate accountability deprive moral choices of enduring significance because nothing finally leaves the universe better or worse.
pro-extinction-undermines-significance.critique: Strongest feature: The extinction scenario vividly raises a legitimate question about enduring consequence, cosmic permanence, and whether ultimate accountability contributes a distinctive dimension of significance. Principal limitation: The inference equivocates among eternal effect, final-state difference, accountability, and objective importance, without showing why temporally located harms, relationships, or achievements cannot genuinely matter. Live burden: The theistic case must defend permanence as a necessary condition for moral significance rather than one valuable kind of significance, and must answer concrete counterexamples involving finite suffering and love. Locked score: The weak performance band reflects direct central-burden relevance and a clearly recoverable concern, but substantial deductions follow from the unsupported permanence requirement, limited contact with secular reasons, unstable terminology, and inadequate representation of finite-value realism.

tags.label: Equivocation
tags.context: The inference shifts among eternal cosmic consequence, accountability, final-state difference, and objective moral significance without establishing that these notions are equivalent.

con-finite-suffering-objectively-matters.words: Kagan argues that torture objectively matters to victims, families, and communities even when their suffering never alters the universe's eventual cosmic endpoint.
con-finite-suffering-objectively-matters.critique: Strongest feature: The victim-centered counterexample directly defeats the inference from absent eternal consequences to absent present importance by identifying unmistakable subjects and relationships affected by torture. Principal limitation: The example establishes that finite suffering matters more readily than it supplies a complete secular metaphysics explaining the stance-independent status of that importance. Live burden: The secular position must connect the compelling case to a general account of objective value, while the theistic position must narrow its claim to a defensible kind of ultimate significance or explain why victim-centered importance is insufficient. Locked score: The very strong performance band reflects exceptional responsiveness, precise scope, coherent counterexample reasoning, strong warrant, and charitable engagement, with only limited deductions for leaving the deeper realist foundation comparatively compressed.

pro-accountability-aligns-prudence.words: Craig argues that divine accountability ultimately harmonizes prudence and morality, whereas naturalism permits self-interest to conflict with morally required sacrifice.
pro-accountability-aligns-prudence.critique: Strongest feature: The proposal identifies a genuine practical tension between moral sacrifice and personal advantage and explains how ultimate accountability could align their eventual outcomes. Principal limitation: It treats prudence, self-interest, and rational authority too interchangeably, then assumes that conflict makes prudence dominant rather than establishing the comparative weight of competing reasons. Live burden: The theistic case must show why secular moral reasons cannot rationally outweigh self-interest and why externally aligned consequences enhance moral authority rather than merely incentivize compliance. Locked score: The weak performance band reflects subsidiary relevance and a recognizable harmonizing mechanism, but substantial deductions remain because the decisive ranking premise is unsupported, central secular claims go unanswered, and the presentation overstates what the mere possibility of prudential conflict establishes.

con-morality-over-prudence.words: Kagan argues that conflict between morality and prudence does not establish self-interest's supremacy because moral reasons may possess greater rational weight.
con-morality-over-prudence.critique: Strongest feature: The reply isolates the missing premise with exceptional economy: conflict between moral and prudential reasons does not determine which category rationally outweighs the other. Principal limitation: It defeats the claimed priority of self-interest more clearly than it supplies a developed account of how categorical moral reasons acquire or exercise superior rational weight. Live burden: The secular position must explain comparative weighting and demanding sacrifice, while the theistic position must argue rather than assume that unresolved divergence between morality and welfare makes moral compliance irrational. Locked score: The very strong performance band reflects precise diagnostic contact, strong coherence, accurate representation, and proportionate argumentative force, with modest deductions because the positive theory of rational priority remains less developed than the successful rebuttal of prudential supremacy.

con-contract-condemns-atrocity.words: Kagan argues that impartial rational bargainers would objectively prohibit killing innocent people, so Nazi atrocities violate ideal contractual terms regardless of actual approval.
con-contract-condemns-atrocity.critique: Strongest feature: The reply clearly separates actual social acceptance from ideal rational agreement and produces a determinate condemnation of victimizing innocent people under the contractual procedure. Principal limitation: The asserted prohibition is plausible but compressed, because the bargaining constraints, derivation, and categorical authority of hypothetical agreement are not demonstrated in detail. Live burden: The secular case must show why every appropriately situated rational bargainer would select the prohibition and why that selection binds actual offenders, while the theistic case must engage ideal rather than conventional agreement. Locked score: The strong performance band reflects direct response, stable scope, practical determinacy, and charitable handling of the convention objection, while deductions remain for abbreviated derivation and the unresolved bridge from correct output to ultimate normative authority.

pro-atrocities-transcendent-criticism.words: Craig distinguishes believing in God from grounding morality in God, arguing that objective criticism of religious atrocities requires a transcendent standard beyond social belief.
pro-atrocities-transcendent-criticism.critique: Strongest feature: The move carefully distinguishes moral knowledge and personal belief from ontological grounding, preventing religious wrongdoing from directly refuting the proposed divine foundation. Principal limitation: Recognizing atrocities as objectively wrong supports realism but does not establish that the needed standard must be divine, especially when secular categorical reasons and ideal agreement are already offered. Live burden: The theistic case must show why transcending actual opinion entails dependence on God and must directly test whether secular criteria can condemn religious and political atrocities without contradiction. Locked score: The mixed performance band reflects a useful clarification, relevant transcultural application, and stable formulation, while substantial deductions remain because the necessity inference is asserted, the strongest secular alternative receives little engagement, and the response does not complete its comparative burden.

con-salvation-accountability-tension.words: Kagan challenges whether salvation through repentance is consistent with ultimate accountability when an evildoer may avoid the punishment personally deserved for wrongdoing.
con-salvation-accountability-tension.critique: Strongest feature: The challenge identifies a precise internal tension among deserved punishment, repentance, salvation, and the promise that wrongdoers ultimately receive appropriate accountability. Principal limitation: It is correctly framed as an apparent difficulty rather than a contradiction, because forgiveness or another justice mechanism could reconcile the doctrines. Live burden: The theistic account must specify how justice remains satisfied when the wrongdoer does not personally bear the penalty, while the challenger must assess whether substitution, restitution, transformation, or mercy answers the original accountability concept. Locked score: The very strong performance band reflects excellent directness, calibrated force, charitable framing, and central relevance, with limited deductions because raising the tension does not itself establish that every coherent account of salvific justice must fail.

pro-salvation-preserves-justice.words: Craig answers that Christ bears sin's deserved penalty, allowing repentant sinners to receive grace while divine justice remains satisfied rather than abandoned.
pro-salvation-preserves-justice.critique: Strongest feature: The reply directly supplies the missing doctrinal mechanism, explaining that punishment is not waived but borne substitutionally while the repentant wrongdoer receives grace. Principal limitation: Internal consistency depends on whether transferring deserved punishment to an innocent substitute is itself just and whether another's suffering constitutes the offender's accountability. Live burden: The theistic case must defend the moral legitimacy, consent, representation, and attribution involved in substitution, while distinguishing satisfaction of a penalty from personal responsibility, restitution, and transformation. Locked score: The very strong performance band reflects exceptional responsiveness, clear mechanism, stable scope, and accurate engagement with the salvation tension, with remaining deductions because the answer resolves formal payment more fully than the underlying ethical objection to vicarious punishment.

pro-disagreement-access-not-truth.words: Craig distinguishes objective moral reality from fallible knowledge, arguing that selfishness and limited access can produce cultural disagreement without eliminating moral truth.
pro-disagreement-access-not-truth.critique: Strongest feature: The ontology-access distinction is explicit, philosophically important, and carefully qualified, showing that disagreement does not logically entail the absence of objective moral facts. Principal limitation: Fallibility and selfishness are plausible explanations but receive limited evidential development, and the distinction alone does not establish reliable access or explain disagreement's recurring patterns. Live burden: The theistic account must provide an epistemology showing when moral judgments reliably track its transcendent standard, while comparing its error mechanisms with secular reflection rather than merely preserving logical compatibility. Locked score: The strong performance band reflects excellent coherence, stable terminology, calibrated scope, and useful subsidiary-burden contact, while deductions remain for compressed cross-cultural evidence, limited reliability analysis, and incomplete movement from possible error to justified moral knowledge.

con-reflective-moral-progress.words: Kagan explains appalling historical codes as delayed recognition of objective truth, with reflective reasoning gradually correcting inherited tendencies and earlier moral error.
con-reflective-moral-progress.critique: Strongest feature: The gradual-discovery model coherently reconciles objective realism with widespread historical error and appropriately presents moral progress as partial rather than automatic or uniform. Principal limitation: The analogy with discovery elsewhere leaves the reliability mechanism and independent criteria for distinguishing genuine correction from changing preference, consensus, or power broadly specified. Live burden: The secular case must identify truth-tracking practices, evidence, and standards that license progress judgments without circularly defining later views as better, while addressing persistent disagreement among reflective agents. Locked score: The strong performance band reflects direct response, sensible calibration, charitable contact, and a coherent compatibility explanation, while deductions remain for abbreviated historical support, an underdeveloped epistemology, and uncertainty about how reflection overcomes rather than reproduces inherited distortion.

con-finite-love-genuine-value.words: Kagan argues that finite loving relationships possess genuine objective value even though death and eventual cosmic extinction prevent their effects from lasting eternally.
con-finite-love-genuine-value.critique: Strongest feature: The loving-relationship counterexample cleanly distinguishes eternal cosmic consequence from genuine objective value and directly targets the rival inference without exaggerating its conclusion. Principal limitation: The example makes finite value highly plausible but leaves the underlying secular metaphysical account of relational value comparatively brief. Live burden: The secular position must generalize from love to a principled account of finite goods, while the theistic position must explain why permanence adds necessity rather than merely duration or an additional kind of significance. Locked score: The very strong performance band reflects outstanding coherence, precision, responsiveness, charity, and representative practical support, with minimal deductions because the counterexample defeats the broad permanence claim more decisively than it independently proves the complete secular foundation.

strengths: Craig presents a recognizable positive foundation in a necessarily holy and loving divine nature rather than relying only on objections to secular realism.
His strongest exchange distinguishes value-bearing capacities from an explanation of their objective value, exposing a genuine unresolved step in Kagan's agency account.
He clearly separates moral ontology from fallible moral access, preserving objective truth despite disagreement and selfishness.
His substitutionary-atonement reply directly supplies a mechanism intended to reconcile salvation with justice rather than evading the doctrinal tension.

blunders.text: The extinction argument moves from absent permanent cosmic effects to absent objective significance without answering the immediate importance of finite suffering and love.

tags.label: Equivocation
tags.context: The argument shifts among cosmic permanence, final-state difference, accountability, and objective significance without establishing their equivalence.

blunders.text: The prudence argument assumes that conflict with self-interest makes morality rationally subordinate, leaving Kagan's comparative-weight objection unanswered.
The divine-lawgiver and atrocity arguments insufficiently engage ideal contractarianism and categorical reasons as objective rather than merely conventional alternatives.

strengths: Kagan defines secular realism through universal categorical reasons and supplies substantive harm-and-help content rather than reducing morality to preference.
His non-contradiction analogy directly challenges the necessity of a personal lawgiver while leaving room for further debate about moral and logical normativity.
His reflective-agency account explains responsibility clearly, and his finite-suffering and finite-love replies decisively separate objective importance from permanence.
His response on prudential conflict precisely identifies that competing reasons do not establish self-interest's rational supremacy.

blunders.text: The categorical-reasons account characterizes objective authority more clearly than it explains the metaphysical source or binding force of that authority.
The ideal-contract proposal leaves perfect rationality, bargaining constraints, determinacy, and the authority of hypothetical agreement materially compressed.
The moral-progress account needs independent truth-tracking criteria to distinguish discovery from later consensus, altered preference, or shifts in power.

novelty.explanation: This integrates Craig's separate value, duty, and accountability claims into one proportionate explanatory thesis.

premises.text: If objective value requires a noncontingent standard, a necessarily loving and just nature offers a unified candidate whose goodness is not created by variable human attitudes or social agreements.

novelty.explanation: This narrows the divine-nature claim to comparative explanatory unity and avoids treating evolutionary origins as a direct defeater.

premises.text: Moral duties often involve claims one person may appropriately address to another, so a personal foundation may explain directed authority and accountability beyond the bare existence of impersonal reasons.

novelty.explanation: This answers the logic analogy by identifying a specific candidate disanalogy rather than presupposing that all requirements need legislation.

premises.text: Finite suffering and love can matter genuinely now while also gaining an additional dimension if persons endure, wrongs remain answerable, and valuable relationships are not erased by extinction.

premises.text: A defensible account of salvation must combine acknowledged responsibility, voluntary divine self-giving, moral transformation, restitution where possible, and mercy rather than treating transferred suffering as sufficient by itself.

conclusion.text: Therefore, the strongest theistic case is not that secular morality is meaningless, but that a necessarily good personal reality may provide a more unified explanation of value, obligation, hope, and justice.

novelty.explanation: This proportionately limits the conclusion to comparative explanatory advantage instead of claiming that finite secular goods do not exist.

newArguments.title: Second-personal moral authority
newArguments.text: Some duties are not merely reasons to improve outcomes; they are claims that victims and communities may address to wrongdoers. A personal moral foundation could explain this second-personal structure by grounding each person's standing in a common source that authorizes mutual accountability. This does not prove that impersonal realism cannot explain directed duties, but it identifies a substantive comparison the law-of-non-contradiction analogy leaves open: logical consistency does not obviously include forgiveness, blame, demand, restitution, or reconciliation between persons.

novelty.explanation: This is a genuinely new second-personal argument connecting directed claims and relational accountability to a personal foundation.

newArguments.title: Explanatory integration test
newArguments.text: Theistic grounding should be assessed by explanatory integration rather than by claiming that every secular moral judgment collapses. One necessarily good reality could connect why persons have worth, why duties bind, why moral knowledge is possible, and why injustice remains answerable. The proposal gains force only if these connections are developed without circular definitions and compared against sophisticated secular realism. Framed this way, the argument survives Kagan's finite-value counterexamples because it seeks a unified explanation of several moral domains, not a denial that finite lives contain genuine goods.

novelty.explanation: This repairs the fragmented pro route by making explanatory integration the comparative criterion while conceding finite secular value.

thesis.text: The AI steelman is that objective moral reasons may be basic features of reality, with harm, agency, impartial justification, and relationships supplying knowable content without divine legislation or eternal consequences.

novelty.explanation: This integrates Kagan's reason-based, substantive, procedural, and finite-value claims into a unified secular realist thesis.

premises.text: Every explanatory system reaches foundational commitments, so treating some normative truths as basic is not uniquely defective unless a rival foundation explains them with fewer or less controversial assumptions.

novelty.explanation: This directly answers Craig's stopping-point challenge by supplying a comparative criterion for permissible foundational facts.

premises.text: Harm, benefit, agency, reciprocity, and impartial justification can operate as mutually checking constraints, reducing dependence on any single intuition or underspecified contractual procedure.

novelty.explanation: This repairs the open boundary conditions in the welfare and ideal-contract accounts through convergent justification.

premises.text: Responsible agents can recognize and answer reasons even when compliance conflicts with self-interest, so practical conflict does not require postmortem incentives to preserve morality's rational authority.

novelty.explanation: This develops the agency and prudence replies into a positive account of reason-responsive responsibility.

premises.text: Objective importance attaches to the condition and relationships of actual sentient beings, making duration relevant to how much good exists but not a prerequisite for any good to exist.

novelty.explanation: This generalizes Kagan's torture and love counterexamples into a principled account of finite value bearers.

conclusion.text: Therefore, secular moral realism can coherently explain objective reasons, duties, responsibility, criticism, and finite significance, although it still owes substantive metaphysical and epistemic development rather than a divine foundation.

novelty.explanation: This preserves the secular route while expressly retaining the foundational and epistemic burdens identified in the locked record.

newArguments.title: Shared foundational stopping points
newArguments.text: The demand for a further explanation cannot selectively disqualify secular value facts while allowing divine goodness to terminate inquiry. If God's nature is called necessarily good, the account must still explain whether goodness is understood independently or defined through that nature. Secular realism may instead treat reasons against torture and reasons to respect persons as foundational. The comparative question is which foundation better systematizes judgments, supports correction, and avoids unexplained transitions. This does not establish secular realism automatically, but it prevents explanatory depth from being measured by unequal stopping rules.

novelty.explanation: This introduces a new parity argument that evaluates divine and secular foundational stopping points by the same explanatory standards.

newArguments.title: Public corrigibility without revelation
newArguments.text: Secular moral inquiry can claim limited reliability through public corrigibility: affected testimony reveals harms, impartial role reversal tests privilege, empirical inquiry corrects factual mistakes, and logical consistency exposes exceptions designed for favored groups. None of these methods guarantees agreement, but together they explain how moral beliefs can improve without assuming that later consensus defines truth. They also supply independent evidence for calling some historical changes progress. This framework strengthens the reflective-discovery account by identifying mechanisms that can challenge inherited preference and power rather than merely redescribing civilization's later judgments as discoveries.

novelty.explanation: This repairs the compressed progress account by specifying public, fallible, truth-directed methods for moral correction.
